prompt: Match each family to what it does.

pairs.right: watches for attacks and triages alerts
attacks with permission to show the gaps

prompt: According to the lesson, what lets people move between the five families?
hint: What do all of them share?

choices.text: A single certification valid for all five
choices.why: No such certificate exists.

choices.text: The shared foundation
choices.why: Right. The vocabulary of this course.

choices.text: A law that requires rotation between roles
choices.why: Nothing obliges anyone to move.

choices.text: Identical daily tasks in every family
choices.why: They differ in what they do all day.

prompt: Which lesson did forensics grow out of, together with lesson 10?

choices.text: Lesson 12, backups and recovery
choices.why: Right. A verified copy is the forensic habit.

choices.text: Lesson 17, the LGPD
choices.why: That one belongs to GRC.

choices.text: Lesson 6, least privilege
choices.why: That grew into AppSec.

choices.text: Lesson 15, the NIST frameworks
choices.why: Another GRC lesson.

prompt: What does a first-line SOC analyst spend most of a shift doing?

choices.text: Triage
choices.why: Right. Close with a note, or escalate.

choices.text: Testing systems inside an agreed scope
choices.why: That is offensive security.

choices.text: Writing new detection rules
choices.why: That is detection engineering, deeper in the tiers.

choices.text: Leading the lessons-learned meeting
choices.why: That is the senior end, incident response.

prompt: Why is triage hard, in the terms of lesson 11?

choices.text: Alerts are written in a foreign language
choices.why: Not the reason the lesson gives.

choices.text: The real alert looks like the noise
choices.why: Right. Judgement under volume.

choices.text: Analysts may not close any alert
choices.why: Closing with a note is most of the work.

choices.text: Alerts arrive only once a week
choices.why: The trouble is the opposite: volume.

prompt: Order the SOC tiers from the first look to the deepest work.
items: tier 3: hunt for what no alert caught
trap: The names vary between SOCs; the order of depth does not.

prompt: What does the client of a penetration test actually pay for?

choices.text: The moment the tester finds the way in
choices.why: A small share of the time, and worthless unexplained.

choices.text: The report
choices.why: Right. Evidence and a recommendation someone can act on.

choices.text: A list of tools the tester used
choices.why: Tools are not what gets fixed.

choices.text: A guarantee that no attacker will ever get in
choices.why: No test can promise that.

prompt: A tester notices a server just outside the agreed scope with an obvious weakness. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Test it only at night, when traffic is low
choices.why: The hour does not create permission.

choices.text: Leave it alone and raise it with the client
choices.why: Right. The scope is the authorisation.

choices.text: Test it quickly, since it helps the client
choices.why: Out of scope, even to be helpful, ends careers.

choices.text: Test it and leave it out of the written report
choices.why: That adds dishonesty to the trespass.

prompt: Match each offensive role to its work.

pairs.right: a defined scope for a set period
new flaws reported to the vendor

prompt: Which skill does the lesson say GRC work builds?

choices.text: Writing exploit code
choices.why: That is not GRC's work.

choices.text: Memorising every clause of ISO 27001
choices.why: Knowing where to look matters more.

choices.text: Configuring firewalls
choices.why: Some came from there; it is not the skill built.

choices.text: Translation
choices.why: Right. Technical to business, and back.

prompt: What separates a good GRC professional from a checkbox filler, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Avoiding conversations with engineers
choices.why: The work is mostly conversation.

choices.text: Owning more certificates than colleagues
choices.why: The lesson does not count certificates.

choices.text: Seeing when a paper control fails
choices.why: Right. Like asking for a restore test.

choices.text: Writing longer policies
choices.why: Length is not the difference.

prompt: Match each GRC role to the lesson it grew from.
hint: The last column of the table.

prompt: Why does a forensic analyst work on a copy rather than the original?

choices.text: The law forbids opening any disk
choices.why: No law says that.

choices.text: Analysing the original changes it
choices.why: Right. And the copy is verified with a hash.

choices.text: The original belongs to the attacker
choices.why: It belongs to the organisation.

choices.text: Copies are faster to read
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

prompt: The record of who held the evidence, when, and what they did with it is the chain of ___.
hint: A word also used for prisoners.

prompt: Lesson 16's checklist, run on every change in the build, is an example of which AppSec task?

choices.text: Developer enablement
choices.why: That is libraries and training.

choices.text: Chain of custody
choices.why: That is a forensic principle.

choices.text: Threat modelling
choices.why: That happens before building.

choices.text: Security testing in the pipeline
choices.why: Right. Found before release, not after.

prompt: Where may you practise attacking a system?

choices.text: On your own systems, or with written permission
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10's difference.

choices.text: On any public site, if nothing is damaged
choices.why: Without authorisation it is a crime, whatever the intent.

choices.text: On a company's site after telling them by phone
choices.why: A phone call is not written authorisation.

choices.text: On a former employer's network you still know
choices.why: Knowing it is not permission.

prompt: Why are CTF competitions and training platforms legal places to practise?

choices.text: The targets are already broken
choices.why: Vulnerable is not the same as authorised.

choices.text: Their servers sit outside Brazil
choices.why: Location does not create permission.

choices.text: Their owners built the targets for it
choices.why: Right. And they publish the scope.

choices.text: Anything in a competition is permitted
choices.why: They publish rules; read them.

prompt: How does the lesson suggest treating certifications?

choices.text: As something to avoid until senior
choices.why: There are entry-level ones.

choices.text: As study structure and a CV filter
choices.why: Right. Useful, and not the skill.

choices.text: As a replacement for a written lab
choices.why: Write-ups show more.

choices.text: As proof that the skill is there
choices.why: Not the skill itself.

prompt: Which of these does every family in this lesson need, according to the last section? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a degree in law
choices.why: Some arrive from law; it is not required.

choices.text: knowing who owns a risk
choices.why: Lessons 2 and 3.

choices.text: writing clearly
choices.why: Getting started said so.

choices.text: telling a real alert from noise
choices.why: Lesson 11.

prompt: Ana found during lesson 12's restore test that the backup skipped the invoices folder. In which family's terms is writing that up most like the work?
hint: Evidence that a control works, or does not.

choices.text: Offensive security: a way in
choices.why: Nobody attacked anything.

choices.text: SOC: an alert in a queue
choices.why: No alert fired; a test found it.

choices.text: GRC: evidence about a control
choices.why: Right. Lesson 13's evidence, and an auditor's question.

choices.text: Forensics: evidence for a court case
choices.why: There was no incident to investigate.
